title: What does the bill expression give for a new order?
description: The bill expression is used for seven coconuts and four kilograms of jaggery, and its two parts are named. Keeko doubts that the value of the expression stays the same for every order.
teaching_notes: One idea: putting numbers in place of the letters gives the value of an expression, and the added parts are its terms. Watch for students who think an expression has one fixed value.

source: Use the expression c × 35 + j × 60 for 7 coconuts and 4 kg of jaggery, and name its two terms
video_script.why: A learner sees that the same expression gives a different value for a different order, and meets the word term for each added part.
video_script.substitution: The book's own expression for the bill, used for seven coconuts and four kilograms of jaggery.
video_script.anchor: {{NAME_2}}'s bill expression, c times thirty five plus j times sixty
video_script.wrong_answer: the value of the expression stays the same
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks one expression has one value; the bill for ten and five was six hundred and fifty, but for seven and four it is four hundred and eighty five.
video_script.payoff_line: {{NAME_2}} must pay four hundred and eighty five rupees

final_answer.value: 485 rupees; the terms are c × 35 and j × 60
final_answer.spoken: the bill is four hundred and eighty five rupees, and the terms are c times thirty five and j times sixty

never_show: the bill 485 before the answer beat
maths_rules: Replace c by 7 and j by 4: 7 × 35 + 4 × 60 = 245 + 240 = 485 rupees.
The two terms are c × 35 and j × 60.
A different c or j gives a different value, so the value of the expression changes.
video_script.design: One idea: replace the letters by numbers to get a value, and the added parts are terms. Assumes the expression for the bill. The expression stays on the stage with its two parts coloured. Wrong idea: the value never changes.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the bill slip of {{NAME_2}} with the coconut line and the jaggery line; an order card of 7 coconuts and 4 kg

marks.p1: the title card From your book arrives
marks.p2: the bill slip with its two lines appears
marks.p3: an order card for seven coconuts and four kilograms is written

narration: <bookmark mark='p1'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='p2'/>It uses the bill of {{NAME_2}}, the cost of the coconuts plus the cost of the jaggery.
<bookmark mark='p3'/>The book asks for the bill of an order of seven coconuts and four kilograms.
Can the same expression be used for this new order?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the expression c × 35 + j × 60 with its two parts coloured differently and a plus sign between them

marks.g1: the expression is written with the plus sign between two coloured parts
marks.g2: the first coloured part is circled
marks.g3: the word term is written under the circled part

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>The bill is written as two parts that are added.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>Each part of an expression that is added is called a term.
<bookmark mark='g3'/>The letters in an expression can take different numbers.

beats.on_screen: Given: expression c × 35 + j × 60 ; c = 7 coconuts, j = 4 kg

marks.gv2: the values for c and j are written beside it

narration: <bookmark mark='gv1'/>Given, the expression is c times thirty five plus j times sixty.
<bookmark mark='gv2'/>The order is seven coconuts and four kilograms of jaggery.

beats.on_screen: To find: the value of the expression ; its two terms

marks.fd2: the second aim is written under it

narration: <bookmark mark='fd1'/>We find the bill for this order from the expression.
<bookmark mark='fd2'/>Then we name the two parts of the expression.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: replace c by 7 and j by 4 ; 7 × 35 + 4 × 60

marks.s1a: c is replaced by 7 and j by 4

narration: <bookmark mark='s1a'/>Replace c by seven and j by four in the expression.
<bookmark mark='s1b'/>It becomes seven times thirty five plus four times sixty.
<bookmark mark='s2a'/>Seven times thirty five is two hundred and forty five.
<bookmark mark='s2b'/>Four times sixty is two hundred and forty.
<bookmark mark='s2c'/>The bill is two hundred and forty five plus two hundred and forty.
<bookmark mark='s3a'/>The first term of the expression is c times thirty five.
<bookmark mark='s3b'/>The second term is j times sixty.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 485 rupees ; terms: c × 35 and j × 60

marks.ans: 485 rupees is boxed beside the two terms

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>{{NAME_2}} must pay four hundred and eighty five rupees.
The two terms are c times thirty five and j times sixty.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: the value never changes, struck out; two bill slips side by side, 650 rupees for 10 and 5, 485 rupees for 7 and 4

marks.d2: the two bill slips appear side by side

narration: <bookmark mark='d1'/>Keeko thinks the value of the expression stays the same, since it is one expression.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>But ten coconuts and five kilograms gave six hundred and fifty rupees. This order gives four hundred and eighty five.
<bookmark mark='d3'/>The expression stays the same, but its value changes when c or j changes.
